top_stories.title: July inflation cools to 3.4%, clearing the way for a Fed hold
points: Consumer Price Index (CPI, the government's main gauge of what households pay for goods and services) rose 3.4% year-over-year in July, matching forecasts and down from 3.5% in June.
Core inflation (which excludes volatile food and energy prices) fell to 2.5%, a third straight monthly decline.
Prediction-market odds of no Fed rate change in September rose to 60% from 45% a week earlier, while rate-hike odds slipped to 34% from 40%.
Bond markets now price roughly one rate cut by year-end, down from three anticipated six weeks ago.
Services inflation remains elevated near 3.2%, keeping Fed officials divided on how fast prices are truly normalizing.
Weak July hiring data added to the case for standing pat, giving policymakers dual signals of cooling prices and softening jobs.

unique_angles.point: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh stayed hawkish, insisting the central bank won't let its 2% inflation target drift to 3%, though investors largely shrugged at the rhetoric.
Lettuce prices hit record lows (down over 40% year-over-year on bumper harvests), a concrete example of food-price deflation undercutting the two-year inflation narrative.
Stock index futures (contracts letting traders bet on where stock prices will be later) traded slightly higher into the print.
Softer inflation plus AI momentum pushed global markets toward record highs.

top_stories.title: AI earnings, not macro data, are driving the market
points: Nebius and CoreWeave each jumped about 19% on strong quarterly results, while the S&P 500 rose just 0.26% on the cooler CPI print.
Nebius revenue surged 454% to $582 million, with its AI cloud business growing more than 5x.
CoreWeave doubled revenue to $2.58 billion (up 112% year-over-year) and booked $25 billion in additional commitments.
Super Micro Computer raised fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $65–72 billion versus Wall Street's $52.5 billion estimate.
Mega-cap tech (the 'Magnificent Seven': Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Tesla, Nvidia, Meta) gained 2–3% as money rotated out of defensive positions.
Semiconductor and hardware names rallied on expectations of sustained AI data-center spending.

unique_angles.point: Tech giants have committed roughly $5 trillion of AI capital expenditure over five years, making a 0.25% shift in the federal funds rate (the interest rate banks charge each other overnight) economically immaterial to their plans.
Market breadth improved as mid-cap growth stocks joined the rally for the first time in three weeks.

top_stories.title: Paramount Skydance dangles CNN sale and a California exit to save $110B Warner Bros. deal
points: Chief legal officer Makan Delrahim said selling CNN is 'on the table' to settle the antitrust suit blocking the $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.
The deal already has clearance from US federal regulators, the UK, EU and China; only the state lawsuit remains.
California AG Rob Bonta and 11 other states argue the combined company — Paramount's studios and CBS News plus HBO, DC Studios and TNT — would raise prices and cut competition.
Paramount faces a $7 million-per-day termination fee if the transaction doesn't close by October 1.
CEO David Ellison told leadership he would move the company out of California unless the state drops its claims, echoing Elon Musk's Tesla/SpaceX shift to Texas.
A relocation to Tennessee, Texas or Georgia could save about $500 million a year in taxes plus billions from selling studio lots.

unique_angles.point: Governor Gavin Newsom, worried about losing Hollywood, is reportedly pushing Bonta's office toward an out-of-court settlement; Paramount has also floated a board to guarantee CNN's editorial independence.
A federal court has set a March trial date on the merger's legality, implying months of costly delay and risk the deal unravels; the states counter that a bigger Paramount would dominate TV and film.

top_stories.title: LA Lakers sold for a record $12.5 billion
points: The purchase, at a record price for a sports franchise, was struck in roughly 24 hours with minimal investment-banker involvement.
Buyers were Thrive Capital founder Joshua Kushner and former Disney CEO Bob Iger, with Mark Walter selling.
Madison Square Garden Sports (MSGS) shares rallied on the read-through to other franchise valuations.

unique_angles.point: The sale helps Walter's TWG Global cut related-party loans at its insurance units, which had drawn Justice Department scrutiny; Iger quipped that avoiding 'hordes, investment bankers and the like' kept talks secret.
Frames the price as evidence wealthy investors treat teams as prestige assets with embedded real-estate and media value.

top_stories.title: Anthropic in talks to buy AI startup Decart for ~$6 billion
points: The AI lab is negotiating a roughly $6 billion acquisition of Decart, one of the sector's larger consolidation moves.
The talks underscore continued investor appetite for artificial-intelligence assets and specialized capabilities.

top_stories.title: South Korea's Kospi flips from bear to bull market in two weeks
points: The Kospi index moved from bear-market territory (down 20%+ from a recent peak) into a technical bull market (up 20%+ from its low) in about two weeks.
The whipsaw reflects short-covering and bargain hunting off oversold levels amid the broader global AI-led rally.

top_stories.title: Energy: oil steady near $75 as Iran pressure builds, US pump prices set an August record
points: Crude held around $75 a barrel, with OPEC production cuts offsetting demand worries.
Oil wavered as traders waited on negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz after the Trump administration reverted to economic pressure on Iran following a failed military campaign.
US average gasoline topped $4 a gallon after August 12 for the first time on record for that date, per GasBuddy.
July gasoline prices fell 2.9% month-over-month but are still up 25% year-over-year.

unique_angles.point: Analyst Tom Kloza expects more supply interruptions and says the final third of the year will be 'considerably more expensive' than prior years.

items.title: Big banks pilot blockchain for everyday trading
points: JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs and Investec are testing blockchain (a shared digital ledger that records transactions across many computers at once) for day-to-day securities trading.

items.title: Nelson Peltz eyes Caesars Entertainment
points: Peltz is reportedly preparing a $34-per-share bid for Caesars (CZR), after Carl Icahn had already made an offer, signaling activist interest in gaming.

items.title: Other headlines

Karoline Leavitt is stepping down as White House press secretary amid broader staff changes.
The US Army is absorbing tactical lessons from Ukraine's drone warfare.

items.title: Treasury yields slip

items.title: US authorizes private-sector offensive cyberattacks
points: The Trump administration will partner with private companies to run offensive cyberattacks abroad against criminal groups targeting Americans, after months of legal groundwork.
The White House warned US systems need stronger defenses against AI-powered cyberattacks (automated intrusions that use machine-learning models to find vulnerabilities faster than human hackers).
The policy extends to private firms operations previously reserved for government agencies.

The US Defense Secretary authorized joint military operations with Colombia against drug gangs and narco-terrorism.

points: Thousands are being recruited to wear head-mounted cameras and motion-tracking gear while doing household chores, generating data to train robots.
Pay is about $315 a month, raising ethical questions since the recordings may automate the workers' own jobs.

items.title: The suit is back in fashion

points: Slowing wage growth is cutting household purchasing power while prices stay elevated, a risk to corporate revenues and stock valuations.

issues.subject: CNN's Corporate Home Thrown Into Question

headlines: Paramount Skydance puts CNN on sale to resolve $110B Warner Bros. merger antitrust lawsuit from California and 11 states, with CEO threatening to relocate company from California if deal stalls past Oct. 1 deadline.
LA Lakers sold for $12.5B as Madison Square Garden Sports (MSGS) rallies on the eye-popping sports team valuation.
South Korea's KOSPI index swung from bear market (down 20% from peak) to bull market (up 20% from bottom) in just two weeks, signaling rapid sentiment reversal.

sections.title: CNN Sale Emerges as Antitrust Fix for Paramount-Warner Bros. Deal
points: 1. Paramount Skydance's chief legal officer Makan Delrahim stated CNN sale is "on the table" to resolve a lingering antitrust lawsuit blocking the $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, which already obtained clearance from U.S. federal regulators, UK, EU, and China.

2. The lawsuit, led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and 11 other states, argues the merged "media behemoth" would raise prices and reduce competition by combining Paramount's production studios and CBS News with Warner Bros.' HBO, DC Studios, and TNT properties.

3. Paramount faces mounting pressure with a $7 million-per-day termination fee if the deal doesn't close by October 1, and executives have publicly discussed relocating operations to Tennessee, Texas, or Georgia to save $500M annually in taxes plus additional billions from studio lot sales.

4. California Governor Gavin Newsom is reportedly concerned about losing Hollywood and is encouraging Attorney General Bonta's office to find an out-of-court settlement, indicating potential political pressure to resolve the dispute.

sections.title: Sports Valuation Spike: Lakers Sold for $12.5B
points: 1. The Los Angeles Lakers were sold for $12.5B, marking one of the largest professional sports team transactions and driving Madison Square Garden Sports (MSGS) stock higher.

2. The sale reflects growing valuations in professional sports franchises as wealthy investors view team ownership as both a prestige asset and a potential long-term investment with real estate and media components.

sections.title: South Korea's Market Swings from Bear to Bull in Two Weeks
points: 1. South Korea's KOSPI index transitioned from bear market territory (down 20% or more from recent peaks) to bull market status (up 20% or more from lows) within a two-week period, indicating extreme volatility and rapid investor sentiment shifts.

2. The sharp reversal suggests either major positive economic news, resolution of geopolitical concerns, or a technical bounce from oversold conditions that triggered short-covering and bargain hunting.

sections.title: Corporate and Technology Developments
points: 1. Anthropic is in talks to acquire AI startup Decart for approximately $6B, continuing the AI sector's consolidation trend as larger players snap up specialized artificial intelligence capabilities.

2. JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, and Investec are testing blockchain (a distributed ledger technology that records transactions across multiple computers) for day-to-day securities trading, signaling mainstream financial institutions' gradual adoption of blockchain infrastructure.
3. SpaceX released Grok 4.6, a frontier AI model focused on visual task processing, and the company's valuation rose following the announcement as investors responded to AI capability advances.

4. Nelson Peltz is reportedly preparing a $34-per-share bid for Caesars Entertainment (CZR), while Carl Icahn previously made an acquisition offer, indicating activist investor interest in the gaming and entertainment sector.

issues.subject: Morning Brief: The Fed catches a break on inflation

headlines: July inflation cooled to 3.4% year-over-year, down from 3.5% in June, giving the Federal Reserve confidence to hold interest rates steady in September rather than raise them.
August gasoline prices hit an all-time high for this date at over $4 per gallon, despite monthly declines, as oil supply disruptions from geopolitical conflict continue to sting consumers.

Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison threatened to relocate the company from California unless the state drops antitrust claims blocking the Warner Bros. Discovery merger, mirroring Elon Musk's Texas strategy.
AI infrastructure stocks surged after strong earnings from CoreWeave and Supermicro, as investors bet on continued growth in data center demand for artificial intelligence.

sections.title: Inflation Eases But Fed Remains Cautious
points: 1. CPI rose 3.4% in July versus year-ago, matching economist expectations and marking the second consecutive month of cooling after June's 3.5%.
2. Market bets shifted heavily toward the Fed holding rates in September rather than raising, with cooler inflation removing pressure for tightening moves.
3. Fed officials remain divided; while the inflation reading offers 'cover to hold,' economists note one good month isn't conclusive proof of sustained progress toward the Fed's 2% target.
4. Weak July jobs numbers compounded the case for holding steady, giving central bankers dual signals—moderating prices and weakening hiring—that argue against rate increases.

sections.title: Energy Costs Hit Historic Peak Despite Monthly Relief
points: 1. National average gasoline prices exceeded $4 per gallon after August 12 for the first time in recorded history for this time of year, according to GasBuddy research.
2. July gasoline prices fell 2.9% month-over-month but remain up 25% year-over-year, showing the lag between short-term commodity relief and cumulative price pain.

3. Analysts expect further oil supply interruptions through the rest of 2026, with chief oil analyst Tom Kloza predicting the final third of the year will be 'considerably more expensive' than previous years.
4. The contrast highlights how aggregate inflation measures mask the persistent sting consumers feel at the pump despite month-to-month declines.

sections.title: Paramount CEO Uses Relocation Threat as Merger Leverage
points: 1. CEO David Ellison told company leadership he would move Paramount Skydance out of California unless the state drops antitrust claims blocking the Warner Bros. Discovery merger.
2. The move echoes Elon Musk's strategy of shifting Tesla and SpaceX operations to Texas to escape regulatory pressure, a tactic other tech firms have adopted via incorporation moves.
3. A federal court set a March trial date for determining the merger's legality, meaning months of costly delays that increase risk the deal unravels or loses shareholder support.

4. Ellison's leverage argument centers on California losing tens of thousands of jobs, media production capacity, and tax revenue, though the states leading the antitrust case maintain a larger Paramount would unfairly dominate TV and film.
